Hello, everyone. I am a writer and scholar of black religion and music. I am finishing a book about the Black Church, the Hammond organ and the AIDS crisis (the impact the crisis had on gospel music). I write primarily about Hammond organists (it's my favorite instrument) but I talk about choir directors and singers too. The book covers a lot of history. 

If you'd be willing to talk to me about a church musician (or, musicians) you knew that died of AIDS-related complications, I'd love to talk to you. Feel free to message me directly.

What church musicians died of AIDS-related complications?

Titles are generated by AI from Meta

Hello, everyone. I am a writer and scholar of black religion and music. I am finishing a book about the Black Church, the Hammond organ and the AIDS crisis (the impact the crisis had on gospel music). I write primarily about Hammond organists (it's my favorite instrument) but I talk about choir directors and singers too. The book covers a lot of history. 

If you'd be willing to talk to me about a church musician (or, musicians) you knew that died of AIDS-related complications, I'd love to talk to you. Feel free to message me directly.

# How Facebook uses the email or mobile phone number on your profile

Copy link

What does Facebook use my data for?

How do I add an email address?

How do I add a phone number?

How do I recover my Facebook account?

I have a different question

 We’re gradually updating people to [Meta Accounts](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.meta.com%2Fhelp%2Fmeta-account%2F876751767182450%3Fhelpref%3Dfaq_content&h=AUC2d646VIyMtibzTqYzAmlXOPeEF8Rs1j_uN-HjKsq6FWZGjfGVGvgTCqhRY8P0_sINAK_pJIK7U_2gLSoKnnUE0TTmBrER4ckkGAbOv4G1LKzI9oNDkopKZoVl8ukQ5MzyuGXG7JgM7Q). You may see either Accounts Center or Meta Account settings as the place to manage your account settings.

## How we use your email address or mobile phone number

We may use your email address or mobile phone number for purposes like:

*   [Helping you log in](https://www.facebook.com/help/283100488694834?helpref=faq_content). If you forget your password, you'll need an updated phone number or email address to reset it. If you forget or [lose access](https://www.facebook.com/help/132243923516844?helpref=faq_content) to the email address or phone number associated with your account, you can use one to look up the other. 
*   Sending you email, WhatsApp and SMS notifications for updates about activity on your account, promotions and account safety. These notifications can help keep your account safe through features like two-factor authentication and alerts about unrecognized logins.
*   Providing and improving ads for you and others. We use your contact information alongside information we get from your activity to help us improve our ads services for everyone within the Facebook community.
*   Some of our security checkpoints can be difficult to pass using assistive technology. If you add a mobile number or email address to your Facebook account, you'll have another way to verify your account if you need to pass any of these checkpoints. Keep in mind that these checkpoints may require internet access. 

By entering your phone number, you authorize your mobile network provider to share data from your account and device to Facebook or its service providers for phone number verification and fraud prevention purposes. Learn more about the data we collect and how we use it in our [Privacy Policy](https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/).

We never sell personal information, including your email address and phone number, to anyone. Keep in mind that you can control who can [see your contact information](https://www.facebook.com/help/117118145038822?helpref=faq_content) and who we can [suggest your profile to](https://www.facebook.com/help/131297846947406?helpref=faq_content) based on your phone number or email address. Learn more about how Facebook uses your phone number and email address in our [Privacy Policy.](https://www.facebook.com/about/privacy)

You may see an email or phone number suggested for you when we ask you to add your contact information. Emails or phone numbers shown in this way will only be added to your account if you choose to [add them](https://www.facebook.com/help/223900927622502?helpref=faq_content).

## How we suggest email addresses or phone numbers

We may suggest an email address or phone number for you based on information we receive from sources such as: 

*   Contact information provided by others on Facebook.
*   An email address or phone number that you entered previously but didn't confirm.
*   Your mobile phone or tablet.

## Reasons for confirming your mobile phone number

We may ask you to confirm your mobile phone number because:

*   You previously [added the phone number](https://www.facebook.com/help/297947214257999?helpref=faq_content) we're asking you to confirm.
*   Time has passed since you last added or updated your phone number.
*   We’ve received information from your device that helps us suggest the number connected to that device.
*   You haven’t added one yet, and we want to show you how.

## More information

*   [Add or remove a mobile phone number.](https://www.facebook.com/help/124895950923762?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Add or remove an email address.](https://www.facebook.com/help/162801153783275?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Adjust how you get notifications.](https://www.facebook.com/help/390022341057202?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Recover your Facebook account if you can't access your account email address or mobile phone number.](https://www.facebook.com/help/132243923516844?helpref=faq_content)

# Information for people who don’t use Meta Products

Copy link

Meta Platforms, Inc. (“**Meta**”, “**we**”, “**our**” or “**us**”) processes your name, mobile phone number and/or your email address if we receive it from our users through the [contact uploading](https://www.facebook.com/help/355489824655936?helpref=faq_content) or [contact syncing](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fhelp.instagram.com%2F1128997980474717%3Fhelpref%3Dfaq_content%26fbclid%3DIwZXh0bgNhZW0CMTAAYnJpZBExdjlialFqV3NOZnlOTW91WnNydGMGYXBwX2lkEDIyMjAzOTE3ODgyMDA4OTIAAR6U-MuSScj0med6_xRXQSqdgvCtCX8_VWIUrM4QGPjMbW5k3FFu9V7EtC4PnQ_aem_5tvGrVuUEjlLnIzZ21wuOA&h=AUAkD247LfJKiR5pk4sdP1bxWIElM7h1IBwWoz7aXaZg7YIKSl54D4WqGi5IXF2zWBvUKH_FxJbdXykEQKOBSsj2XNjFVfzEfQPiaLYA4NOwYupeAbswddMUa03HymsUeMaWelvTl-Qf7Q) feature available on Facebook, Messenger or Instagram (“**Contact Uploading**”). We process this information even if you are not a user of Facebook, Messenger or Instagram and/or don’t have an account with us (a “**Non-User**”).

## About Contact Uploading and how it works

When a user uses Contact Uploading and grants us access to their mobile device’s address book or their Google Account, we will access and upload the names, phone numbers and email addresses in their address book or their Google Account on a daily basis to our servers, including those of both users of Facebook, Messenger and/or Instagram and other contacts who are not users or don’t have an account (i.e., Non-Users).

## What information is collected about Non-Users?

We collect the name, mobile phone number and/or email address of a user's contacts.

## How do we use a Non-User’s information?

Contact Uploading is an optional feature where users can choose to upload their mobile device's or Google Account’s address book to Facebook, Messenger and/or Instagram. We process the names, phone numbers and/or e-mail addresses in the address book to see if any of the numbers or email addresses belong to users. If a user’s contact is also on Facebook, Messenger and/or Instagram, we can suggest this contact on Facebook as someone to send a friend request to in the Facebook user’s [People You May Know](https://www.facebook.com/help/1163341187771886?helpref=faq_content) or as a suggested account to follow on Instagram. Users can also invite Non-Users to join Facebook, Messenger and/or Instagram via text or email.

Contact Uploading also allows us to suggest a Non-User who joins as a user of Facebook as a friend to add for the user through [People You May Know](https://www.facebook.com/help/1163341187771886?helpref=faq_content) or as a suggested account to follow on Instagram.

Finally, we will also use the address books uploaded to investigate suspicious activity on the [Meta Products](https://www.facebook.com/help/1561485474074139?helpref=faq_content) and keep our platform safe and secure. We also conduct business intelligence and analytics using the address books uploaded to accurately count people and users of the [Meta Company Products](https://www.facebook.com/help/195227921252400?helpref=faq_content).

Meta shares information we collect, infrastructure, systems and technology with the other [Meta Companies](https://www.facebook.com/help/111814505650678?helpref=faq_content). We share Non-Users’ data with other Meta Companies to be able to provide the contact import feature and for the purposes set out above.

We retain Non-User’s personal information for as long as needed to provide the Contact Importer feature to users and for the purposes described above. In certain cases, we need to keep your contact information for longer, including after you ask us to erase it. This includes for legal reasons such as to respond to a legal request or comply with applicable law, for regulatory or litigation matters, to prevent harm or for safety, security and integrity purposes. The length of time we need to keep it will depend on the specific reason.

## How Non-Users can exercise their rights

We enable Non-Users to exercise their rights under applicable laws. To exercise your rights, contact us using the contact information below.

You can learn more about how privacy works [on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/privacy/center) and on [Instagram](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fhelp.instagram.com%2F196883487377501%3Fhelpref%3Dfaq_content&h=AUAkD247LfJKiR5pk4sdP1bxWIElM7h1IBwWoz7aXaZg7YIKSl54D4WqGi5IXF2zWBvUKH_FxJbdXykEQKOBSsj2XNjFVfzEfQPiaLYA4NOwYupeAbswddMUa03HymsUeMaWelvTl-Qf7Q), and in the [Facebook Help Center](https://www.facebook.com/help/).

We hope that we can satisfy any queries a Non-User may have about the way in which we process their personal information. In some countries you may also be able to contact the Data Protection Officer for Meta Platforms, Inc., and depending on your jurisdiction, you may also contact your local Data Protection Authority (“DPA”) directly.

[Click here](https://www.facebook.com/contacts/removal) if you have a question about the rights you may have.

## How we transfer information

We share the information we collect globally, both internally across our offices and data centers, and externally with our partners, service providers, and vendors. Because Meta is global, with users, partners and employees around the world, transfers are necessary for a variety of reasons, including so we can operate and provide the services described in this Data Notice.

Non-User information will be transferred or transmitted to, or stored and processed in:

*   Places we have infrastructure or data centers, including the United States, Ireland, Denmark and Sweden, among others
*   Countries where Meta Products are available
*   Other countries where our partners, service providers and vendors are located outside of the country where you live, for purposes as described in this Data Notice.

We rely on appropriate mechanisms for international data transfers. For example, for information we collect:

*   We utilize [standard contractual clauses](https://www.facebook.com/help/566994660333381?helpref=faq_content) approved by the European Commission and by other relevant authorities.
*   We rely on determinations from the European Commission, and from other relevant authorities, about whether other countries have [adequate levels of data protection](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fec.europa.eu%2Finfo%2Flaw%2Flaw-topic%2Fdata-protection%2Finternational-dimension-data-protection%2Fadequacy-decisions_en%3Ffbclid%3DIwAR37fTNaCt1VimAmH4D7rS95WKolCqb0Tk1cEfwl0MqvN14TL6NHPqb3XQY&h=AUAkD247LfJKiR5pk4sdP1bxWIElM7h1IBwWoz7aXaZg7YIKSl54D4WqGi5IXF2zWBvUKH_FxJbdXykEQKOBSsj2XNjFVfzEfQPiaLYA4NOwYupeAbswddMUa03HymsUeMaWelvTl-Qf7Q).
*   We use equivalent mechanisms under applicable laws that apply to data transfers to the United States and other relevant countries.

## United States Regional Privacy Notice

If you are a United States resident, you can learn more about your consumer privacy rights by reviewing the [United States Regional Privacy Notice](https://www.facebook.com/legal/policy/ccpa).

## Contact us

If you have questions about this Notice, or have questions, complaints or requests regarding your information, please [use this form](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fhelp.meta.com%2Fsupport%2Fprivacy%3Ffbclid%3DIwZXh0bgNhZW0CMTAAYnJpZBExdjlialFqV3NOZnlOTW91WnNydGMGYXBwX2lkEDIyMjAzOTE3ODgyMDA4OTIAAR6bFxAraBcfHDvVx3P5lBRE6kQrchRRV8QRwvadxagW9bcRKn_8J8STJrb2PQ_aem_smi4tSSHTL1ruZChKMxOEA&h=AUAkD247LfJKiR5pk4sdP1bxWIElM7h1IBwWoz7aXaZg7YIKSl54D4WqGi5IXF2zWBvUKH_FxJbdXykEQKOBSsj2XNjFVfzEfQPiaLYA4NOwYupeAbswddMUa03HymsUeMaWelvTl-Qf7Q).

Hello, everyone. I am a writer and scholar of black religion and music. I am finishing a book about the Black Church, the Hammond organ and the AIDS crisis (the impact the crisis had on gospel music). I write primarily about Hammond organists (it's my favorite instrument) but I talk about choir directors and singers too. The book covers a lot of history. 

If you'd be willing to talk to me about a church musician (or, musicians) you knew that died of AIDS-related complications, I'd love to talk to you. Feel free to message me directly.

![Image 1: Muse](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/brand/muse-logo.svg)
# Muse, AI that gets it done for you Muse[Video 1](https://l.facebook.com/videos/avatars/hatch_connecting.mp4)[Video 2](https://l.facebook.com/videos/avatars/hatch_working.mp4), AI that gets it done for you sorts your email books reservations shops for you saves you money manages calendars builds fitness plans gets it done for you sorts your email![Image 2](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-envelope.webp)books reservations![Image 3](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-airplane.webp)shops for you![Image 4](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-cart.webp)saves you money![Image 5](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-piggybank.webp)manages calendars![Image 6](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-calendar.webp)builds fitness plans![Image 7](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/b-01.webp)gets it done for you

## Built around your whole life

Give Muse a goal or task and it handles the rest, from saving money and improving your health to smart shopping and helping you strengthen your relationships.

[Video 3](https://scontent.xx.fbcdn.net/o1/v/t6/f2/m421/AQPvdntV2G814fVexG62mHy9MLAFz-IUx2_276pwlTOScjlG7403bT1NxrxgW2yToPZR5BOsHoRWgC3EQGGX.mp4?_nc_sid=9c7e41&_nc_ht=scontent.xx.fbcdn.net&ccb=17-1&_nc_gid=NJaZ5pvwwdSsf99Zrx-y6A&edm=AIlawRcEAAAA&_nc_zt=28&oh=00_AQN1WPiIYleZ4DUCccBgxKhQc_L1J86LkkAKR4LVRdBuyw&oe=6AEC19AE#t=1)

### Every Muse user shares their own computer in the cloud with their Muse.

Muse Secure VM is a persistent, isolated Linux computer with a full browser that you and your agent can use to complete tasks, allowing you to intervene at any point. It's your computer and your browser, with the storage, CPU, and memory to handle real work.

![Image 8: Floating browser, search, map, calendar, and confirmation panels](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/browser.webp)![Image 9: Floating browser, search, map, calendar, and confirmation panels](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/browser-dark.webp)

### Designed around the way you already communicate

Chat with your agent in the same way you message with other people, using the Muse app on mobile, Mac, or directly in WhatsApp. There's no learning curve, just tell Muse what you want to get done.

![Image 10: A chat on a phone where the agent has filled out a school form, shown beside a laptop](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/messaging.webp)![Image 11: A chat on a phone where the agent has filled out a school form, shown beside a laptop](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/messaging-dark.webp)

### Stay in control of what your agent does

Approve actions your agent takes on your behalf before they happen, like sending emails and making purchases. See a complete audit trail of everything your agent has done (and what it's planning to do).

![Image 12: Floating purchase, message, activity, permission, and decision controls](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/approvals.webp)![Image 13: Floating purchase, message, activity, permission, and decision controls](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/approvals-dark.webp)

### Your data is kept secure and private

Save your logins to a secure credential store Muse can't see, with 1Password integration coming soon. When shopping, a one-time card number is generated at checkout so your real card stays hidden from the merchant and your agent. Eligible purchases are covered by [Link's purchase protections](https://link.com/protections), a first for AI agents, and your conversations are not shared with Meta's ad systems.

![Image 14: A vault, privacy shield, masked credential, security control, and virtual card](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/secure-storage.webp)![Image 15: A vault, privacy shield, masked credential, security control, and virtual card](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/secure-storage-dark.webp)

### Proactively helps with your goals and suggests ideas

Muse helps you stay on top of things, takes tasks and projects off your plate, and turns long-term goals into real progress. It learns from conversations, reflects on what matters and gets sharper, coming back with ideas built around what you actually need, ready to act on them under your direction.

![Image 16: Floating checklist, calendar, route, progress, and idea panels](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/goals.webp)![Image 17: Floating checklist, calendar, route, progress, and idea panels](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/goals-dark.webp)

### Connects to your apps and builds its own tools

Connect the apps you use daily, like email, calendar, and Instagram. You decide what your agent can see and what it can do. If a task needs a tool that doesn't exist, your agent builds it for you.

![Image 18: Connected app, messaging, media, cloud, calendar, and automation tiles](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/connectors.webp)

## Get the most out of your Muse

A guided tour of Muse, from setting a first goal to seeing it through.

![Image 19: Product designer presenting a guided tour of Muse](https://l.facebook.com/images/hatch/landing/product-walkthrough-cover.png)

## Learn more about Muse

Explore the choices behind Muse and how it is built to deserve your trust.

### [How We Designed Muse When Muse works, it feels like magic. These are the product choices that make the experience possible.](https://introducing.muse.ai/)### [How We Built Safety Into Muse Muse is built for privacy, safety, and security. Learn how these principles shape every part of the product.](https://security.muse.ai/)### [Muse for Business Meet the AI agent that works for your small business and keeps jobs moving between your decisions.](https://l.facebook.com/business)

## Ready to try Muse?

Memories of St. Vincent's Hospital during the AIDS crisis in the 1980s

Titles are generated by AI from Meta

View looking out from my friend John Tenenbaum's hospital room at St. Vincent's Hospital in 1988. He died later that year. I remember wondering if it was appropriate to take advantage of the photo-op when he was sick in bed. Nonetheless, the scene and image are stuck in my mind, and I'm glad I have it all these years later. RIP old friend. Photo: Brian Street, 1988.

# The Catholic Hospital That Pioneered AIDS Care

![Image 4: Oloughlin (1)](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Oloughlin-1-205033-80x80.jpg)by[Michael J. O’Loughlin](link_47)January 24, 2020

### Share this:

*   [Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)Facebook](https://www.americamagazine.org/faith/2020/01/24/catholic-hospital-pioneered-aids-care/)
*   [Share on X (Opens in new window)X](https://www.americamagazine.org/faith/2020/01/24/catholic-hospital-pioneered-aids-care/)
*   [Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window)Email](mailto:?subject=%5BShared%20Post%5D%20The%20Catholic%20Hospital%20That%20Pioneered%20AIDS%20Care&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.americamagazine.org%2Ffaith%2F2020%2F01%2F24%2Fcatholic-hospital-pioneered-aids-care%2F&share=email)

![Image 5: OLoughlinFeature_2_02-03-20](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/OLoughlinFeature_2_02-03-20-221625.png?fit=1200%2C776&ssl=1)

St. Vincent's Hospital, New York City, 2006 (Wikimedia Commons)

One fall afternoon, I stood on a small island of green located in the crosshairs of three hectic New York City streets. It was rush hour, the sun beginning to set. Harried New Yorkers hurried through the park on their way from work to happy hour. A gay couple sat holding hands on a bench. A few children screamed and laughed, running away from their exhausted-looking parents. It is possible many of the people in the New York City AIDS Memorial Park at St. Vincent’s Triangle were unaware of its purpose, which is to memorialize two things: the more than 100,000 New Yorkers who have died from AIDS-related complications since the early 1980s, and the hospital where many of those people spent their final days.

[_**[Listen to the new podcast from America Media, “Plague: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church”]**_](https://www.americamagazine.org/plague [link_48])

I walked around the perimeter and spotted a series of dark gray, circular medallions, about the size of manhole covers, embedded in the faded red pavers that circle the park. The discs form a series of concentric circles. On one, the outermost circle, in all capital letters, is printed, “FORMER SITE OF SAINT VINCENT’S HOSPITAL 1849-2010.” The next ring reads, “THE SISTERS OF CHARITY FOUNDED THE HOSPITAL TO CARE FOR THE POOR AND DISADVANTAGED.” An image of a woman appears in the middle, identifiable by her distinctive bonnet as a member of the Sisters of Charity. I kept walking and came across the marker I had been looking for. The center circle contains the image of a ribbon. Around it is printed “INTERNATIONAL AIDS EPIDEMIC 1980s” and around that “IN 1984 SAINT VINCENT’S OPENED THE FIRST AND LARGEST AIDS WARD ON THE EAST COAST.”

### A Historic Refuge

Saint Vincent’s Hospital served the poor and indigent for as long as it existed. In its earlier days, sisters took care of victims from a massive cholera epidemic. People who had been aboard the Titanic when it sank were taken here. Not far from the site of the twin towers of the World Trade Center, the hospital treated victims of the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. But I was interested in learning more about what happened here in the 1980s, when this Catholic hospital became synonymous with care for people with AIDS, especially lower-income gay men and drug users who could not afford fancier hospitals. Today it is not so easy to see that an iconic hospital once stood in this area. Most of the buildings that were once part of the hospital campus have been converted into multi-million dollar condominiums. Still, there are some small visual reminders of what this place once was. A sign above a doorway reads “Nurses Entrance,” with a sculpture of a Sister of Charity. “St Vincent’s Hospital” is etched above the main entrance of another building.

### ‘They Were There’

As I walked around the campus with a couple of friends, carrying a microphone for recording interviews, a man with silver hair spotted us. He had something he wanted to say and walked over. Tom Bernarden introduced himself; he said he had lived in the neighborhood for decades. We told him we were interested in the history of the hospital. He told us about his admiration for the Sisters of Charity of New York and why Saint Vincent’s was so important to the L.G.B.T. community during the height of the H.I.V. and AIDS crisis.

“I lost all my friends, all right. You understand? I’m 24 when I move in here. I’m 70” today, he told us. When asked about the sisters, he paused for a moment. “They were there,” he said, recalling how many other people turned their backs to a community in need. “They were there.” Mr. Bernarden, a local tour guide who describes himself as the unofficial mayor of the park, had a few less complimentary things to say about the Catholic Church, mostly about money. But he also told complete strangers how much he admired the Catholic sisters who ran Saint Vincent’s, praising them for caring for the sick when everyone else vanished.

“I lost all my friends, all right. You understand?”

Mr. Bernarden and I spoke for awhile. The things he told me prompted some questions. How did this Catholic hospital, which had already been run by sisters for more than a century, become a haven for gay men during the AIDS crisis? Part of the answer is geography. Saint Vincent’s was located in an area where many gay men lived. But it goes beyond that. The iconic place of Saint Vincent’s in the story of the AIDS crisis is due to pushing from activists who knew the hospital could do better, a pioneering gay doctor hired to open the hospital’s AIDS clinic and a group of sisters who saw people and need and asked themselves, “What can we do to help?”

### ‘A Cry for Help’

Seeking answers, I headed up to the Bronx, where the College of Mount Saint Vincent has sat overlooking the Hudson River since 1847. The leadership team of the Sisters of Charity of New York has offices on campus, and I was there to meet Sister Karen Helfenstein. She had trained at Saint Vincent’s nursing school, rose through the ranks and eventually became a top hospital administrator. She served as the vice president for mission during the height of the H.I.V. and AIDS crisis. Sister Karen recalls that, early on, there was friction between the hospital and the gay community.

Sister Karen recalls that, early on, there was friction between the hospital and the gay community.

One September evening in 1989, a group of activists from the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power, a radical protest group better known as ACT UP, took over the waiting area in the hospital’s emergency room. Tensions had been rising in the gay community over the church’s prohibition against condoms. Doctors and public health officials had urged people at risk of acquiring H.I.V. to use condoms to lessen the risk. But Catholic hospitals in New York City were not allowed to distribute condoms because of the church’s prohibition on artificial birth control. It appeared, at first, that the protest in the E.R. was about this issue; one of the activists had placed condoms on a statue of the risen Christ. Some hospital staff wanted to press charges because of that disrespectful act. But Sister Karen and the other Sisters of Charity took a step back. “I really wasn’t angry. I knew those people were struggling,” she said. “I felt it was a cry for help.”

Saint Vincent’s was a Catholic hospital, so it provided medical care that was in line with church teaching. Part of that is to care for the poor, which included gay men and drug users with H.I.V. and AIDS. It also meant following church teaching on sexual ethics, which did not permit condoms.  From Times Wire Services 

OGDEN, Utah—Clair Harward, an AIDS victim whose story of remorse, loneliness and excommunication from the Mormon Church created a national response, has died alone in a bed at St. Benedict’s Hospital here.

A spokesman said he had asked for a private funeral service before he died Sunday of complications of the nearly always fatal acquired immune deficiency syndrome.

Harward, 26, gained national attention when the Standard-Examiner of Ogden published his story, including an account of his excommunication from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Advertisement

But Mormon Bishop Brent S. Farr said Harward worked during the past few months to regain a closeness with the church.

Farr, who helped Harward after he was excommunicated by a bishop’s court in another Ogden ward, said Harward had no regrets about making his story public.

“A number of people from the LDS Church and people from all different denominations were very sympathetic,” Farr said. “It was an unfortunate situation that he was caught up in, and I feel sorry for him and his family.”

Advertisement

Harward was diagnosed as having AIDS in August, 1984. He went to his Mormon lay bishop for counsel but he said the bishop told him to give up his gay friends and identify his past sexual partners.

Harward said it would have been “unethical” to identify his gay friends. “When I need my friends most, they’re asking me to be alone.”

The Mormon Church views homosexuality as a sin in the same degree with adultery and premarital sex, church spokesman Jerry Cahill said.

# AIDS Victim Excommunicated by Mormon Church Court Dies

L.A. Times Archives

March 19, 1986 12 AM PT 

*

 From Times Wire Services 

OGDEN, Utah—Clair Harward, an AIDS victim whose story of remorse, loneliness and excommunication from the Mormon Church created a national response, has died alone in a bed at St. Benedict’s Hospital here.

A spokesman said he had asked for a private funeral service before he died Sunday of complications of the nearly always fatal acquired immune deficiency syndrome.

Harward, 26, gained national attention when the Standard-Examiner of Ogden published his story, including an account of his excommunication from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Advertisement

But Mormon Bishop Brent S. Farr said Harward worked during the past few months to regain a closeness with the church.

Farr, who helped Harward after he was excommunicated by a bishop’s court in another Ogden ward, said Harward had no regrets about making his story public.

“A number of people from the LDS Church and people from all different denominations were very sympathetic,” Farr said. “It was an unfortunate situation that he was caught up in, and I feel sorry for him and his family.”

Advertisement

Harward was diagnosed as having AIDS in August, 1984. He went to his Mormon lay bishop for counsel but he said the bishop told him to give up his gay friends and identify his past sexual partners.

Harward said it would have been “unethical” to identify his gay friends. “When I need my friends most, they’re asking me to be alone.”

The Mormon Church views homosexuality as a sin in the same degree with adultery and premarital sex, church spokesman Jerry Cahill said.

Memories of St. Vincent's Hospital during the AIDS crisis in the 1980s

Titles are generated by AI from Meta

View looking out from my friend John Tenenbaum's hospital room at St. Vincent's Hospital in 1988. He died later that year. I remember wondering if it was appropriate to take advantage of the photo-op when he was sick in bed. Nonetheless, the scene and image are stuck in my mind, and I'm glad I have it all these years later. RIP old friend. Photo: Brian Street, 1988.

Sam Stoia

I was a 21 year old seminarian for the Catholic Archdiocese of Newark and assigned to do my Clinical Pastoral Education (CPE) at St. Vincent's hospital. The experience was so jarring leaving me feeling ill suited to minister to anyone going through that. I remember visiting with one patient whose friend/roommate/lover arrived to visit him later that normal. The patient asked his friend why he was so late and the guy told him that he had to find a new laundry in a different neighborhood, because their regular laundry closed apparently out of fear of contracting AIDS from people's clothing. I left the seminary soon after.

# Plague: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church

In “Plague,” journalist Michael O’Loughlin investigates the untold stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church from the 1980’s. Mike is America’s national correspondent and he has covered Catholicism for more than a decade. Mike is also gay and Catholic—and he is curious how others manage this sometimes complex identity. Through dozens of interviews and archival research, he has found that no time in modern history was more volatile for gay Catholics than the height of the AIDS epidemic.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/AppleLogo.png?resize=20%2C20&ssl=1) Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/plague-untold-stories-of-aids-and-the-catholic-church/id1488020105 [link_45])

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/SpotifyLogo.png?resize=20%2C20&ssl=1) Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/6pV8qX40nrj4t6Q1QI9kIi?si=4dc9f08c14c4456c [link_46])

In “Plague,” journalist[Michael O’Loughlin](link_47)investigates the untold stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church.

You can listen to “Plague” on**Apple Podcasts**[here](link_45), on**Google Play**[here](link_48), or on**Spotify**[](link_49)[here](link_49).The podcast, which now includes eight original episodes, won awards from the Catholic Media Association, the Religion News Association and the National LGBT Journalists Association.

Mike is**America**’s national correspondent and he’s covered Catholicism for more than a decade. Mike is also gay and Catholic—and he’s curious how others manage this sometimes complex identity.

Through dozens of interviews and archival research, he’s found that no time in modern history was more volatile for gay Catholics than the height of the AIDS epidemic.

Mike met with people who were right there, in the middle of the early days of the HIV and AIDS epidemic in the United States. People who fought, worked and grieved their ways through this trying time. You can listen to the trailer and first two episodes below, and subscribe to the podcast to get each new episode as it is released.

In addition to “Plague,” you can read more of Mike’s coverage on the topic in his book, “[Hidden Mercy: AIDS, Catholics, and the Untold Stories of Compassion in the Face of Fear](link_50),” and original reporting at**America**, including:

_“PLAGUE: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church” is made possible by the generosity of Mark A. McDermott and Yuval David, whose gift honors and supports all LGBTQ+ persons and allies past and present._

Our dedicated staff is producing groundbreaking content every day, including the “Plague” podcast. This production would not be possible without the support of our subscribers. Please continue to support our work by[subscribing to**America**](link_51).

# Features

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Marcelli-distributing-food-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/features/2026/10/05/st-francis-breadline-new-york-homeless/ [link_45])

Posted in[Features](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/features/)
## [How the St. Francis Breadline provides food to NYC’s homeless—without judgment](link_45)

![Image 5: Jim McDermott](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/Jim-McDermott-298816-96x96.jpg)![Image 6: Avatar photo](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/cropped-image0-scaled-1-96x96.jpeg)Story by[Jim McDermott](link_46)

Photographer[David Gonzalez](link_47)

[October 5, 2026 October 5, 2026](link_45)

Since 1930, the St. Francis Breadline has stayed open though blackouts, blizzards and rainstorms, serving without judgment everyone who comes.

[![Image 7: A priest carries a monstrance as members of a Catholic group take part in a procession near the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview, Ill., Oct. 11, 2025.](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CSPL-DAILY-ACCESS-ICE-FACILITY-1819993-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/features/2026/09/21/broadview-ice-immigrants-communion/ [link_48])

Posted in[Features](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/features/)
## [In Chicago, a Catholic community organizer is using faith to resist ICE](link_48)

![Image 8: Avatar photo](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/cropped-Heather-Gary_2024-80x80.jpg)by[Heather Grennan Gary](link_49)[September 21, 2026 September 21, 2026](link_48)

Joanna Arellano-Gonzalez helped found the Coalition for Spiritual and Public Leadership in 2017. Now the group finds itself in court with the Trump administration.

[![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260323T1422-STFRANCIS-VENERATION-IN-ASSISI-ENDS-1815596-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/features/2026/09/10/in-the-footsteps-of-st-francis-how-my-travels-through-italy-brought-me-closer-to-a-beloved-saint/ [link_50])

Posted in[Features](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/features/)
## [In the footsteps of St. Francis: How my travels through Italy brought me closer to a beloved saint](link_50)

![Image 10: Screen Shot 2019-12-30 at 3](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Screen-Shot-2019-12-30-at-3.15.21-PM-325764-80x80.png)by[Stephanie Saldaña](link_51)[September 10, 2026 September 29, 2026](link_50)

All of life was a pilgrimage for St. Francis of Assisi. It only made sense, 800 years after his death, that I would go on my own pilgrimage in search of him.

[![Image 11](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Untitled-design-43.png?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/features/2026/09/08/us-bishops-trump-immigration-iran/ [link_52])

Posted in[Features](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/features/)
## [The U.S. bishops are speaking out forcefully on politics—and finally being heard](link_52)

![Image 12: sawyer-headshot](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/sawyer-headshot-316422-80x80.jpg)by[Sam Sawyer, S.J.](link_53)[September 8, 2026 September 10, 2026](link_52)

Prompted by the beginnings of both Leo XIV’s papacy and the second term of Donald J. Trump, the bishops are using their voice in a new way.

[![Image 13](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Keenan-w-firefighters-in-dress-uniform-Octavio-Duran-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/features/2026/08/13/fdny-chaplain-911/ [link_54])

Posted in[Features](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/features/)
## [How an F.D.N.Y. chaplain was formed by 9/11](link_54)

![Image 14: Avatar photo](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/cropped-28-80x80.jpg)by[Edward Desciak](link_55)[August 13, 2026 September 8, 2026](link_54)

As a young man, Chris Keenan befriended Mychal Judge, O.F.M. He never expected to follow in his footsteps.

[![Image 15: Parker Baudo (center), a student in the Mount Sion program at Brother Rice High School in Chicago, interacts with peer mentors. ](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/TLG1224.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/features/2026/08/13/catholic-schools-students-special-needs/ [link_56])

Posted in[Features](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/features/)
## [Meet the Catholic schools serving students with special needs](link_56)

![Image 16: john david jd long garcia-3292 copy crop](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/john-david-jd-long-garcia-3292-copy-crop-172339-80x80.jpg)by[J.D. Long García](link_57)[August 13, 2026 August 20, 2026](link_56)

Because Catholic education should be available to all.

# Arts & Culture

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/640px-Rilke_in_Moscow_by_L.Pasternak_1928-e1774040033805.jpg?resize=640%2C438&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/arts-culture/2026/03/20/finding-a-lenten-vulnerability-in-rilkes-letters-to-a-young-poet/ [link_45])

Posted in[Arts & Culture](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/arts-culture/)
## [Finding a Lenten vulnerability in Rilke’s ‘Letters to a Young Poet’](link_45)

![Image 5: nick_photo(1)](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/nick_photo1-134052-scaled-80x80.jpg)by[Nick Ripatrazone](link_46)[March 20, 2026 March 20, 2026](link_45)

I inherited many books from my older brothers—esoteric books from the 1970s on running and weightlifting, and Pietro di Donato’s classic novel Christ in Concrete, about an Italian immigrant family of laborers shattered by the death of their patriarch. But my favorite is Letters to a Young Poet, by Rainer Maria Rilke. It is a […]

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/MonkeyTrial.jpg?resize=1200%2C817&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/01/15/review-the-scopes-monkey-trial-and-church-state-tensions/ [link_47])

Posted in[Arts & Culture](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/arts-culture/), [Books](link_48)
## [Review: The ‘Scopes Monkey Trial’ and church-state tensions](link_47)

![Image 7: Tom_Deignan](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Tom_Deignan-284977-80x80.jpg)by[Tom Deignan](link_49)[January 15, 2026 January 15, 2026](link_47)

Brenda Wineapple’s ‘Keeping the Faith: God, Democracy, and the Trial That Riveted a Nation’—about the famous Scopes “monkey trial,” is timely. Then again, church-state conflicts simply never go away in the United States.

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/RobReinerTribute.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/film/2025/12/17/rob-reiners-gift-finding-humanity-both-on-and-off-the-screen/ [link_50])

Posted in[Arts & Culture](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/arts-culture/), [Film](link_51)
## [Rob Reiner’s gift: Finding humanity—both on and off the screen](link_50)

![Image 9: Screen Shot 2024-07-25 at 2](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Screen-Shot-2024-07-25-at-2.53.02-PM-422973-80x80.png)by[William Gualtiere](link_52)[December 17, 2025 December 17, 2025](link_50)

The Reiners, so many agreed, were not the type of couple who would sit down. They used their influence and voices to make a difference and had a multigenerational impact.

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/USCCB.jpg?resize=1000%2C665&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2025/12/11/review-the-u-s-church-today-and-tomorrow/ [link_53])

Posted in[Arts & Culture](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/arts-culture/), [Books](link_48)
## [Review: The U.S. church today—and tomorrow](link_53)

![Image 11: Cosacchi](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Cosacchi-827703-80x80.jpg)by[Daniel Cosacchi](link_54)[December 11, 2025 December 11, 2025](link_53)

‘Reclaiming American Catholicism,’ coming in at nearly 400 pages, is a comprehensive and meticulous synopsis of many of the ills that are plaguing the church in the United States.

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Einhorn.jpeg?resize=864%2C648&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2025/12/11/review-slavery-and-american-jewish-history/ [link_55])

Posted in[Arts & Culture](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/arts-culture/), [Books](link_48)
## [Review: Slavery and American Jewish history](link_55)

![Image 13: Screen Shot 2022-08-11 at 2](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Screen-Shot-2022-08-11-at-2.48.12-PM-316970-80x80.png)by[Kevin M. Doyle](link_56)[December 11, 2025 December 18, 2025](link_55)

The Jewish people in America have long punched above their demographic weight. Consider how deprived our science, music, letters, film and law would be absent the contributions of Abraham’s stock. Owing to this and all the discredited drivel about the American slave trade’s supposed Jewish hub, a fresh, thoughtful treatment of Jews and America’s original […]

[![Image 14](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/20220608T1210-SEASON-OF-CREATION-1716133-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2025/12/11/review-a-world-inundated-by-trash/ [link_57])

Posted in[Arts & Culture](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/arts-culture/), [Books](link_48)
## [Review: A world inundated by trash](link_57)

## Hidden Mercy

### AIDS, Catholics, and the Untold Stories of Compassion in the Face of Fear

#### By [Michael J. O'Loughlin (Author)](https://www.broadleafbooks.com/store/author/7987/Michael-J-O-Loughlin)

The 1980s and 1990s, the height of the AIDS crisis in the United States, was decades ago now, and many of the stories from this time remain hidden: A Catholic nun from a small Midwestern town packs up her life to move to New York City, where she throws herself into a community under assault from HIV and AIDS. A young priest sees himself in the many gay men dying from AIDS and grapples with how best to respond, eventually coming out as gay and putting his own career on the line. A gay Catholic with HIV loses his partner to AIDS and then flees the church, focusing his energy on his own health rather than fight an institution seemingly rejecting him.

Set against the backdrop of the HIV and AIDS epidemic of the late twentieth century and the Catholic Church's crackdown on gay and lesbian activists, journalist Michael O'Loughlin searches out the untold stories of those who didn't look away, who at great personal cost chose compassion--even as he seeks insight for LGBTQ people of faith struggling to find a home in religious communities today.

This is one journalist's--gay and Catholic himself--compelling picture of those quiet heroes who responded to human suffering when so much of society--and so much of the church--told them to look away. These pure acts of compassion and mercy offer us hope and inspiration as we continue to confront existential questions about what it means to be Americans, Christians, and human beings responding to those most in need.

Continue the conversation with the[_Hidden Mercy_ Discussion Guide](https://ms.broadleafbooks.com/downloads/HiddenMercy_StudyGuide.pdf)--perfect for book clubs, church groups, and individual study.

# Endorsements

Previous

"A superbly researched, beautifully written and vividly presented portrait of an overlooked time in modern history. An important book about a key part of Catholic and American history that had to be written."

James Martin, S.J., _New York Times_ bestselling author of _Building a Bridge: How the Catholic Church and the LGBT Community Can Enter Into a Relationship of Respect, Compassion, and Sensitivity_

**"**With the precision and drive of an expert investigative journalist, the heart of a poet and the soul of a faithful, gay Catholic conflicted by his own spiritual home, his quest for answers about what the Church did, and did not do, in the mysterious and terrifying beginnings of AIDS in America unearths tragic yet beautiful stories of love and death that may have been lost without this magnificent and passionate documentary."

Jeannie Gaffigan, author of _When Life Gives You Pears: The Healing Power of Family, Faith, and Funny People_

"Michael O'Loughlin sets his sights on an aspect of recent American history and culture too little examined. _Hidden Mercy_ will cause discussion, argument, and maybe recommitment to an ideal of faith in action that can still play out in our day. And a good thing too."

Gregory Maguire, _New York Times_ bestselling author of _Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West_

**"**Michael J. O'Loughlin offers a moving personal history as well as a well written and reported account of the brave priests and nuns--queer and straight alike--that jeopardized their own career and standings with the church by merely treating LGBTQ Catholics with dignity during the height of the AIDS crisis."

Michael Arceneaux, _New York Times_ bestselling author of _I Can't Date Jesus: Love, Sex, Family, Race, and Other Reasons I've Put My Faith in Beyoncé_ and _I Don't Want To Die Poor_

**"**O'Loughlin introduces us to so many unsung heroes of the AIDS crisis, and their lives vividly showcase the compassion and the cruelty that coexist in one community. A harrowing and deeply personal story."

Molly Worthen, associate professor of history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, _New York Times_ contributing opinion writer, and author of _Apostles of Reason: The Crisis of Authority in American Evangelicalism_

**"**Love - much like the power of community - really does stand at the center of _Hidden Mercy_. O'Loughlin never loses sight of that, and queer history is better because of it."

Xorje Olivares, host of the podcast "Queer I am Lord"

**"**Compulsively readable, vigorous and alive, full of searching, complicated, tough-minded, loving people."

Paul Lisicky, author of _Later_ and _The Narrow Door_

**"**With care and curiosity, O'Loughlin weaves a compelling narrative that exists at the intersection of faith and sexuality. What follows is a story that is at times funny, surprising, and ultimately restores some of my own faith that people can and will show up for each other."

Tobin Low, editor at "This American Life" and co-creator of the podcast "Nancy"

"_Hidden Mercy_ unburies the lost testimonies of American Catholic priests and nuns who dared cross into the no man's land between queerness and religion at the height of the AIDS crisis. Punks of the collar, renegades of the cloth, they risked excommunication in the earliest days of the 'gay cancer' and found religious justification to provide a kind of forbidden care."

Robert W. Fieseler, author of _Tinderbox: The Untold Story of the Up Stairs Lounge Fire and the Rise of Gay Liberation_

"Much has been written about how the Catholic Church failed us in the worst years of the AIDS pandemic. Michael O'Loughlin's deep reporting finds a much richer narrative."

David France, author of _How To Survive a Plague_

**"**Michael O'Loughlin beautifully captures the complexity and richness of Catholic responses to AIDS in the USA of the 1980's and 1990's. Both the compassion and the cruelty."

James Alison, author of _Faith Beyond Resentment: Fragments Catholic and Gay_

**"**O'Loughlin's book is a work of resurrection. He unearths and brings to life lives long hidden, overlooked, and forgotten but so constitutive of the early struggle for hope, survival, dignity, and solidarity."

James Keenan, S.J., Canisius Professor of theology at Boston College and author of _Catholic Ethicists on HIV/AIDS Prevention_

# Plague: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church

In "Plague" journalist Michael O'Loughlin investigates stories of the AIDS epidemic and the Catholic Church. Mike is America’s national correspondent and he’s covered Catholicism for more than a decade. Mike is also gay and Catholic—and he’s curious how others manage this sometimes complex identity. No time in modern history has been more volatile for gay Catholics than the height of the AIDS epidemic. So he spent the last few years interviewing people who were right in the middle of it. People who fought, worked and grieved through it.

Play

## Episodes

1.   [Episode 1 ### Surviving the AIDS crisis as a gay Catholic Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In this episode of "Plague," Michael O'Loughlin tells the story of David Pais, whose journey exemplifies the experience of many gay Catholics who were personally affected by the AIDS epidemic in the early days. He describes the role his faith played helping him cope with his own diagnosis—and his struggle as he walked away from the church in anger. You can learn more about "Plague" at americamag.org/plague. You can find Mike on Twitter @mikeoloughlin. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit megaphone.fm/adchoices 41m ![Image 3: The Town with Matthew Belloni](https://podcasts.apple.com/assets/artwork/1x1.gif)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/surviving-the-aids-crisis-as-a-gay-catholic/id1488020105?i=1000458312508) 
2.   [Episode 2 ### The Catholic hospital that pioneered AIDS care Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In the second episode of “Plague,” Mike asks: how did a Catholic hospital become a safe haven for the gay community? It turns out, the path wasn’t straightforward. This episode tells the story of St. Vincent's Hospital, run by the Sisters of Charity of New York. Featured voices include Dr. Ramon Torres, the young gay physician hired by the sisters to lead the AIDS clinic; Gerri Wells, an ACT UP protester; and Karen Helfenstein, S.C., the soft-spoken sister who served as St. Vincent’s vice president for mission. Learn more at americamag.org/plague Learn more about your ad choices. Visit megaphone.fm/adchoices 35m ![Image 4: The Town with Matthew Belloni](https://podcasts.apple.com/assets/artwork/1x1.gif)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-catholic-hospital-that-pioneered-aids-care/id1488020105?i=1000458974966) 
3.   [Episode 3 ### The cost of AIDS ministry to a gay priest Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! Early in the AIDS epidemic, there was little in the way of medical treatment available. But spiritual guidance and accompaniment was in high demand. Patients had questions similar to those anyone else with a terminal illness might have: Are my affairs in order? Am I reconciled with my loved ones? Am I ready to die? The third episode of “Plague” tells the story of the AIDS crisis from the perspective of a priest, trying to figure out what he could do to help. Father William Hart McNichols, a gay priest who was an early volunteer at St. Vincent’s. Bill talks to Mike O’Loughlin about his mission to accompany hundreds of men in their final days, and how his vocation as an artist came into play. “It was everything I ever wanted to be as a priest,” Bill told Mike. “And I got to do it all with these people.” Learn more at www.americamag.org/plague. You can follow Mike on Twitter @mikeoloughlin. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit megaphone.fm/adchoices 37m ![Image 5: The Town with Matthew Belloni](https://podcasts.apple.com/assets/artwork/1x1.gif)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-cost-of-aids-ministry-to-a-gay-priest/id1488020105?i=1000459639208) 
4.   [Episode 4 ### A gay Catholic Church in the Castro Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In the fourth episode of “Plague,” Mike visits a Catholic Church in the Castro–San Francisco’s LGBT neighborhood–that transformed itself during the 80s and 90s into what parishioners called a “gay church.” It took the delicate balance of an innovative pastor, committed gay parishioners, and open-minded old ladies to bring life to the now iconic church. But the parish didn’t just survive. It transformed itself into a place where the neighborhood it served could rely on it for spiritual sustenance and physical help during the height of the HIV and AIDS crisis. As one member put it to us, Most Holy Redeemer became a place that helped save souls, and save lives. In short, it became a model for what a parish should be. Learn more at www.americamag.org/plague. You can follow Mike on Twitter @mikeoloughlin. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit megaphone.fm/adchoices 40m ![Image 6: The Town with Matthew Belloni](https://podcasts.apple.com/assets/artwork/1x1.gif)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/a-gay-catholic-church-in-the-castro/id1488020105?i=1000460436293) 
5.   [Episode 5 ### A Catholic Sister learns to serve people with AIDS Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In the fifth episode of "Plague," Mike visits the small Midwestern city of Belleville, Illinois, where a Catholic Sister broke ground in the 1980s by opening an organization to provide services for people living with HIV and AIDS. Though she was a trained ICU and ER nurse, Sister Carol Baltosiewich had much to learn about the disease before she could help treat it. So she journeyed to New York City with another sister to volunteer at Catholic hospitals on the front lines of the AIDS crisis. That experience dramatically changed Sister Carol's perspective. She witnessed firsthand the suffering people with AIDS experienced, along with their partners and family members. But it was the deep love present amidst the suffering that truly changed her. She would come to realize that ministering to people with HIV and AIDS first required a sincere self-examination. As she put it, "You can't even deal with AIDS until you first face your own prejudices and biases." Sister Carol returned to Belleville and got to work. She set up a helpline to answer questions about HIV and AIDS, which turned into a highly respected AIDS service organization known as "Bethany Place". Learn more at www.americamag.org/plague. You can follow Mike on Twitter@mikeoloughlin. You can listen to “Plague” on Apple Podcasts here, on Google Play here, or on Spotify here. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit megaphone.fm/adchoices 36m ![Image 7: The Town with Matthew Belloni](https://podcasts.apple.com/assets/artwork/1x1.gif)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/a-catholic-sister-learns-to-serve-people-with-aids/id1488020105?i=1000461014439) 
6.   [Episode 6 ### AIDS, the Catholic Church and LGBT issues today Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In the series finale of ‘Plague,’ Mike looks at what’s happening in the church in HIV and AIDS care today and then reflects on comments and questions from listeners about the ongoing debates over LGBT issues in the Catholic Church. In Rustenburg, South Africa, where today AIDS is disproportionately impacting girls and young women, a Catholic bishop and religious sister promote education and empowerment, and offer a pro-life argument for the use of condoms in HIV and AIDS prevention. Then, returning to the United States, Mike speaks with medical doctor and Jesuit priest Jon Fuller about the stubbornly high rate of HIV within marginalized communities, and how remembering the AIDS crisis of the 1980s and 90s can break down intergenerational barriers between people living with HIV and AIDS. Finally, the series wraps with a reflection on the key takeaways from the podcast—and a consideration of what’s at the heart of the broader debates over LGBT issues in the Catholic Church today. Bill talks to Mike O’Loughlin about his mission to accompany hundreds of men in their final days, and how his vocation as an artist came into play. “It was everything I ever wanted to be as a priest,” Bill told Mike. “And I got to do it all with these people.” Learn more at www.americamag.org/plague. [Plague: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church](https://open.spotify.com/show/6pV8qX40nrj4t6Q1QI9kIi)  Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In the fourth episode of “Plague,” Mike visits a Catholic Church in the Castro–San Francisco’s LGBT neighborhood–that transformed itself during the 80s and 90s into what parishioners called a “gay church.” It took the delicate balance of an innovative pastor, committed gay parishioners, and open-minded old ladies to bring life to the now iconic church. But the parish didn’t just survive. It transformed itself into a place where the neighborhood it served could rely on it for spiritual sustenance and physical help during the height of the HIV and AIDS crisis. As one member put it to us, Most Holy Redeemer became a place that helped save souls, and save lives. In short, it became a model for what a parish should be. Learn more at www.americamag.org/plague. [Plague: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church](https://open.spotify.com/show/6pV8qX40nrj4t6Q1QI9kIi)  Please support "Plague" by getting a digital subscription to America: tap or click here! In the fifth episode of "Plague," Mike visits the small Midwestern city of Belleville, Illinois, where a Catholic Sister broke ground in the 1980s by opening an organization to provide services for people living with HIV and AIDS. Though she was a trained ICU and ER nurse, Sister Carol Baltosiewich had much to learn about the disease before she could help treat it. So she journeyed to New York City with another sister to volunteer at Catholic hospitals on the front lines of the AIDS crisis. That experience dramatically changed Sister Carol's perspective. She witnessed firsthand the suffering people with AIDS experienced, along with their partners and family members. But it was the deep love present amidst the suffering that truly changed her. She would come to realize that ministering to people with HIV and AIDS first required a sincere self-examination. As she put it, "You can't even deal with AIDS until you first face your own prejudices and biases." Sister Carol returned to Belleville and got to work. She set up a helpline to answer questions about HIV and AIDS, which turned into a highly respected AIDS service organization known as "Bethany Place". Learn more at www.americamag.org/plague. ## [Remembering Peter Henriot, a Jesuit scholar who helped put Catholic social teaching on the map](https://www.americamagazine.org/catholic-book-club/2026/09/29/peter-henriot-jesuit-obituary-catholic-social-teaching/)

![Image 5: keane_0](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/keane_0_0-388967-80x80.jpg)by[James T. Keane](https://www.americamagazine.org/author/james-t-keane/)[September 29, 2026 September 29, 2026](https://www.americamagazine.org/catholic-book-club/2026/09/29/peter-henriot-jesuit-obituary-catholic-social-teaching/)

While U.S. Catholics might remember Peter Henriot, S.J., best for his social justice advocacy, he was better known in the minds of many for his decades of service to the church in Africa.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20140409T0900-ROWAN-541436.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/25/review-roman-williams-solidarity/)

Posted in[Books](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/books/)
## [Review: Rowan Williams on bringing back solidarity](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/25/review-roman-williams-solidarity/)

![Image 7: Avatar photo](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/cropped-paul-contino-80x80.jpg)by[Paul J. Contino](https://www.americamagazine.org/author/paul-j-contino/)[September 25, 2026 September 25, 2026](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/25/review-roman-williams-solidarity/)

In ‘Solidarity,’ Rowan Williams offers one imperative that reverberates through his book: If we are to recover a sustainable spirit of solidarity, we must work, both interpersonally and politically, to go beyond too-easy, sometimes performative declarations like “I feel for you and stand with you.”

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/AP26259521942605-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/catholic-book-club/2026/09/22/annie-dillard-obituary-catholic-book-club/)

Posted in[Catholic Book Club](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/catholic-book-club/)
## [Annie Dillard: Our 20th-century Thoreau, nature writer and theologian](https://www.americamagazine.org/catholic-book-club/2026/09/22/annie-dillard-obituary-catholic-book-club/)

![Image 9: keane_0](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/keane_0_0-388967-80x80.jpg)by[James T. Keane](https://www.americamagazine.org/author/james-t-keane/)[September 22, 2026 September 23, 2026](https://www.americamagazine.org/catholic-book-club/2026/09/22/annie-dillard-obituary-catholic-book-club/)

Annie Dillard on converting to Catholicism: “You go to a Catholic church, and there are people of all different colors and ages, and babies squalling. You’re taking a stand with these people. You’re saying: ‘Here I am. One of the people who love God.’”

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-2172939942-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/10/review-memory-keepers-death-and-grief-in-brother-epistles/)

Posted in[Books](https://www.americamagazine.org/category/books/)
## [Review: Memory-keepers, death and grief in ‘Brother Epistles’](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/10/review-memory-keepers-death-and-grief-in-brother-epistles/)

![Image 11: CMMOB2](https://www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/CMMOB2-282272-scaled-80x80.jpg)by[Cynthia-Marie Marmo O'Brien](https://www.americamagazine.org/author/cynthia-marie-marmo-obrien/)[September 10, 2026 September 16, 2026](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/10/review-memory-keepers-death-and-grief-in-brother-epistles/)

We think of letters as a two-way form of communication: They go to and fro in the world, from one writer to the reader, who becomes the writer of the next letter. But sometimes we write letters that are not returned in a traditional way. In Brother Epistles: A Sister’s Memoir, Shanda McManus does just […]

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/iStock-2262362503-scaled.jpg?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/10/review-rebecca-gayle-howell-revisits-the-book-of-genesis/)

## [Review: Rebecca Gayle Howell revisits the Book of Genesis](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/10/review-rebecca-gayle-howell-revisits-the-book-of-genesis/)

![Image 13: nick_photo(1)](https://americamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/nick_photo1-134052-scaled-80x80.jpg)by[Nick Ripatrazone](https://www.americamagazine.org/author/nick-ripatrazone/)[September 10, 2026 September 10, 2026](https://www.americamagazine.org/books/2026/09/10/review-rebecca-gayle-howell-revisits-the-book-of-genesis/)

View looking out from my friend John Tenenbaum's hospital room at St. Vincent's Hospital in 1988. He died later that year. I remember wondering if it was appropriate to take advantage of the photo-op when he was sick in bed. Nonetheless, the scene and image are stuck in my mind, and I'm glad I have it all these years later. RIP old friend. Photo: Brian Street, 1988.

# Plague: Untold Stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church

In “Plague,” journalist Michael O’Loughlin investigates the untold stories of AIDS and the Catholic Church from the 1980’s. Mike is America’s national correspondent and he has covered Catholicism for more than a decade. Mike is also gay and Catholic—and he is curious how others manage this sometimes complex identity. Through dozens of interviews and archival research, he has found that no time in modern history was more volatile for gay Catholics than the height of the AIDS epidemic.

View looking out from my friend John Tenenbaum's hospital room at St. Vincent's Hospital in 1988. He died later that year. I remember wondering if it was appropriate to take advantage of the photo-op when he was sick in bed. Nonetheless, the scene and image are stuck in my mind, and I'm glad I have it all these years later. RIP old friend. Photo: Brian Street, 1988.

 From Times Wire Services 

OGDEN, Utah—Clair Harward, an AIDS victim whose story of remorse, loneliness and excommunication from the Mormon Church created a national response, has died alone in a bed at St. Benedict’s Hospital here.

A spokesman said he had asked for a private funeral service before he died Sunday of complications of the nearly always fatal acquired immune deficiency syndrome.

Harward, 26, gained national attention when the Standard-Examiner of Ogden published his story, including an account of his excommunication from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Advertisement

But Mormon Bishop Brent S. Farr said Harward worked during the past few months to regain a closeness with the church.

Farr, who helped Harward after he was excommunicated by a bishop’s court in another Ogden ward, said Harward had no regrets about making his story public.

“A number of people from the LDS Church and people from all different denominations were very sympathetic,” Farr said. “It was an unfortunate situation that he was caught up in, and I feel sorry for him and his family.”

Advertisement

Harward was diagnosed as having AIDS in August, 1984. He went to his Mormon lay bishop for counsel but he said the bishop told him to give up his gay friends and identify his past sexual partners.

Harward said it would have been “unethical” to identify his gay friends. “When I need my friends most, they’re asking me to be alone.”

The Mormon Church views homosexuality as a sin in the same degree with adultery and premarital sex, church spokesman Jerry Cahill said.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Following is a list of notable performers of rock and roll music or rock music, and others directly associated with the music as producers, songwriters or in other closely related roles, who have died in the 1990s. The list gives their date, cause and location of death, and their age.

Rock music developed from the rock and roll music that emerged during the 1950s, and includes a diverse range of subgenres. The terms "rock and roll" and "rock" each have a variety of definitions, some narrow and some wider. In determining criteria for inclusion, this list uses as its basis reliable sources listing "rock deaths" or "deaths in rock and roll", as well as such sources as the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/HollyMonument.jpg/250px-HollyMonument.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HollyMonument.jpg)

Monument at the crash site of the airplane carrying [Buddy Holly](link_3), [The Big Bopper](link_4), and [Ritchie Valens](link_5); "[The Day the Music Died](link_6)".

The following is a list of notable performers of [rock and roll](link_7) music or [rock music](link_8), and others directly associated with the music as producers, songwriters or in other closely related roles, who have died. The list gives their date, cause and location of death, and their age.

Rock music developed from the rock and roll music that emerged during the 1950s, and includes a diverse range of subgenres. The terms "rock and roll" and "rock" each have a variety of definitions, some narrow and some wider. In determining criteria for inclusion, this list uses as its basis reliable sources listing "rock deaths" or "deaths in rock and roll", as well as such sources as the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](link_9).

**Mark Leighton a bassist for [The Yummy Fur](link_47) who was listed in The Club has assured me he is alive and well - My apology to Mark for this error.**

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The following is a list of notable performers of [rock and roll](link_2) music or [rock music](link_3), and others directly associated with the music as producers, songwriters or in other closely related roles, who have died in the 1980s. The list gives their date, cause and location of death, and their age.

Rock music developed from the rock and roll music that emerged during the 1950s, and includes a diverse range of subgenres. The terms "rock and roll" and "rock" each have a variety of definitions, some narrow and some wider. In determining criteria for inclusion, this list uses as its basis reliable sources listing "rock deaths" or "deaths in rock and roll", as well as such sources as the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](link_4).

This is a [dynamic list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Dynamic_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists") and may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness. You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/List_of_1980s_deaths_in_popular_music "Special:EditPage/List of 1980s deaths in popular music") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a [dynamic list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Dynamic_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists") and may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness. You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/List_of_2000s_deaths_in_popular_music "Special:EditPage/List of 2000s deaths in popular music") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

The following is a list of notable performers of [rock and roll](link_2) music or [rock music](link_3), and others directly associated with the music as producers, songwriters or in other closely related roles, who have died in the 2000s. The list gives their date, cause and location of death, and their age.

Rock music developed from the rock and roll music that emerged during the 1950s, and includes a diverse range of subgenres. The terms "rock and roll" and "rock" each have a variety of definitions, some narrow and some wider. In determining criteria for inclusion, this list uses as its basis reliable sources listing "rock deaths" or "deaths in rock and roll", as well as such sources as the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](link_4).

**June Scopes - Died 1-?-2008 - Liver disease ( Country - Rock ) She was 70 years old - Singer - Was a member of Wild Honey.**

**Rick Wright - Died 1-?-2008 ( Rock ) Guitarist - Was a member of [Brutus And The Bullies](http://pnwbands.com/bullies.html).**

**Dennis Clifton (Dennis Allen Clifton) - Died 1-1-2008 in Florence, AL, U.S. - Cancer ( Jazz - Bluegrass ) Born 1-28-1953 - Singer, songwriter, guitarist and studio engineer - Was a member of Surprise Package and FCC (Funky Communications Commission) (They did, "Baby I Want You") and Cornbread Red - Produced Iron Horse.**

**Robert L'Herbier (Robert Joseph Samson) - Died 1-1-2008 - Illness ( Pop ) Born 2-5-1921 in Levis - Singer and songwriter - Canadian Association Of Broadcasters Hall Of Fame Inductee.**
